constraints: The use cases are supported by managed AWS AI services.
The team wants to minimize model-training and infrastructure operations.
The design must still protect input data and measure output quality.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed APIs reduce operations but may constrain model choice, customization, throughput, or data residency.
details.errorCorrection: A custom platform is not automatically justified, object storage does not infer, and a database does not replace a model.
details.mechanismOrProperty: AWS provides managed services for specific modalities, each with its own inputs, outputs, quotas, regions, security controls, and quality behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The architect maps classification, transcription, and translation to separate service contracts and tests accuracy and latency with representative data.

messages.text: Custom infrastructure adds training, serving, patching, and model-lifecycle work before a fit assessment.
Object storage stores data and does not perform arbitrary inference by itself.
A database stores and queries data but does not implement the required model behavior.

feedback.reason: Purpose-built managed AI services can satisfy common inference needs without forcing the team to own model training and serving infrastructure.

options.text: Evaluate purpose-built managed AI services first, then validate quality, privacy, quotas, latency, and integration requirements for each use case.
Build and operate a separate custom deep-learning platform for every use case before testing managed services.
Run all workloads in an object bucket because storage services automatically perform inference.
Use a relational database as the model because SQL queries replace inference and evaluation.

prompt: A team needs image classification, speech transcription, and text translation but has no machine-learning specialists. Which architecture decision is most appropriate?

constraints: The team needs managed training jobs and repeatable artifacts.
Training data is stored in Amazon S3.
The model will be evaluated before deployment.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed training still requires data governance, feature quality, experiment tracking, cost controls, and a promotion policy.
details.errorCorrection: An untracked laptop run is not a reliable training pipeline, DNS checks are not training, and queues do not train or measure models.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A training job defines inputs, compute, algorithm or framework, outputs, and execution configuration; artifacts can be evaluated and stored for later deployment.
details.scenarioApplication: The team versions the S3 data location and code or image, records metrics, and promotes only a model that passes fraud-detection quality checks.

messages.text: Untracked local execution makes reproducibility, capacity, security, and promotion difficult.
Route 53 health checks observe endpoints and do not execute model training.
SQS transports messages and provides no training algorithm or accuracy guarantee.

feedback.reason: SageMaker AI provides managed jobs and artifacts that support repeatable training and controlled promotion.

options.text: Use Amazon SageMaker AI training jobs with versioned data, explicit algorithm or framework configuration, output artifacts, and evaluation gates.
Run an untracked training script on a developer laptop and copy whichever model file was produced most recently.
Use Amazon Route 53 health checks to train the model whenever a DNS endpoint responds.
Use Amazon SQS as the training engine because a queue guarantees model accuracy.

prompt: A company must train a fraud model on labeled data and repeat the training process when new data arrives. Which service is the best managed starting point?

constraints: The caller expects an immediate prediction response.
The model must be deployed behind an authenticated service endpoint.
Capacity and model versions must be observable.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Real-time endpoints incur serving capacity and require scaling, version, timeout, and fallback behavior to be designed explicitly.
details.errorCorrection: S3 is durable storage rather than a low-latency serving layer, CloudTrail records activity, and SQS is asynchronous transport.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The endpoint hosts a deployed model behind an invocation API and can be configured for instance capacity, scaling, access, monitoring, and deployment strategies.
details.scenarioApplication: The fraud API invokes the endpoint with authorized credentials, monitors latency and errors, and rolls out a new model only after validation.

messages.text: Loading a full model from object storage per request adds latency and lacks a managed serving lifecycle.
CloudTrail is an audit service and does not perform inference.
A queue decouples work and cannot directly satisfy a synchronous prediction response.

feedback.reason: A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint is designed for synchronous model inference with managed deployment and capacity controls.

options.text: Deploy the approved model to a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint and configure capacity, access control, monitoring, and a controlled rollout.
Store the model in S3 and tell the API to read the entire model for every request without a serving endpoint.
Use a CloudTrail trail as the prediction endpoint because audit records provide low-latency inference.
Put the model in an SQS message and return the queue URL as the synchronous prediction.

prompt: A fraud API requires synchronous predictions with predictable latency and a model that stays available while traffic varies. Which serving approach should be evaluated?

constraints: The workload is generative text inference.
The team wants a managed model access layer.
Prompts, outputs, data handling, and guardrails must be governed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed model access reduces infrastructure work but does not guarantee factuality, cost, latency, model availability, or safe output without application controls.
details.errorCorrection: An unmanaged public host creates security and operations risk, S3 Select is object querying, and DNS routing does not generate content.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Bedrock exposes model inference and related controls through AWS APIs, while the application remains responsible for authorization, prompts, output handling, and workload governance.
details.scenarioApplication: The support service uses an IAM-scoped role, selects an approved model, applies guardrails and retrieval controls, and monitors latency and quota behavior.

messages.text: An unpatched public model host violates the stated managed and governed operating requirements.
S3 Select filters object data and is not a foundation-model inference service.
Route 53 routes requests and has no content-generation capability.

feedback.reason: Amazon Bedrock provides managed access to foundation models without requiring the team to operate model-serving GPU infrastructure.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon Bedrock for managed foundation-model access, while designing model selection, IAM, guardrails, logging, quotas, and retrieval boundaries.
Use an internet-facing EC2 instance with an unpatched model image and no identity boundary because generative models need unrestricted access.
Use Amazon S3 Select as the foundation model because filtering objects produces generated answers automatically.
Use Route 53 weighted records to generate text by assigning percentages to DNS records.

prompt: A support application needs to generate answers from a foundation model, and the team does not want to provision GPU instances or manage the model runtime. Which service should be evaluated first?

constraints: The input is image or video content.
The team needs managed analysis rather than a custom computer-vision stack.
Results must be handled as application decisions and may require human review.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Managed analysis reduces model operations but requires validation of supported formats, accuracy, privacy, quotas, and false-positive handling.
details.errorCorrection: Polly synthesizes speech, RDS stores relational data, and SQS only transports the work.
details.mechanismOrProperty: The service accepts supported image or video inputs and returns analysis results that the application can evaluate against confidence and business policies.
details.scenarioApplication: The upload workflow stores the original securely, invokes analysis, routes uncertain cases for review, and avoids treating a confidence score as an unconditional business decision.

messages.text: Polly converts text to speech and does not classify image content.
RDS provides relational storage and query capabilities, not image recognition.
A queue can decouple an analysis request but does not perform analysis itself.

feedback.reason: Rekognition is purpose-built for managed image and video analysis use cases such as labels and moderation.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon Rekognition APIs for image or video analysis, then define confidence thresholds, retention, privacy, and review behavior.
Use Amazon Polly because speech synthesis automatically identifies objects in uploaded images.
Use Amazon RDS because relational indexes automatically classify pixels and video frames.
Use an SQS queue alone because queuing an image is equivalent to analyzing it.

prompt: An application must detect labels and moderate images uploaded by users. Which AWS capability is the most direct fit?

constraints: The input is scanned or rendered document content.
The workflow needs structured extraction rather than only raw object storage.
Extracted fields must be validated before a claim is approved.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Extraction results require confidence thresholds, exception handling, privacy controls, and possibly human review for important decisions.
details.errorCorrection: Translate changes language, CloudFront caches content, and DynamoDB Streams reports item changes rather than performing OCR.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Textract analyzes supported document inputs and returns extracted text and structural relationships that an application can consume.
details.scenarioApplication: The claims service stores the source document, invokes the appropriate synchronous or asynchronous operation, validates confidence and required fields, and only then applies business rules.

messages.text: Translation is not document structure extraction and cannot replace OCR for forms and tables.
CloudFront distributes content and does not parse scanned documents into fields.
DynamoDB Streams contains database change records, not document pixels or OCR results.

feedback.reason: Textract is designed to extract printed text and structured elements such as forms and tables from documents.

options.text: Use Amazon Textract for document text, form, and table extraction, then validate the extracted fields before downstream decisions.
Use Amazon Translate because language translation automatically preserves form fields and table structure for claims.
Use Amazon CloudFront because edge caching converts scanned pages into structured claim records.
Use Amazon DynamoDB streams as the OCR engine because stream records contain the pixels from every document.

prompt: A claims workflow must extract text, forms, and tables from scanned documents before sending the fields to a business rules engine. Which managed service is the best fit?

constraints: The input is recorded speech.
The output must be text that can be indexed and reviewed.
Recordings and transcripts contain sensitive customer data.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Speech recognition quality depends on audio, language, speakers, vocabulary, and configuration; sensitive transcripts need retention and access controls.
details.errorCorrection: Polly synthesizes speech from text, EBS snapshots back up volumes, and WAF filters web requests.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Transcribe accepts supported audio or video input and returns a transcript with service-specific configuration and result behavior.
details.scenarioApplication: The contact center starts a job from protected storage, restricts access to recordings and transcripts, and checks output quality before automated action.

messages.text: Polly performs text-to-speech, which is the reverse direction from transcription.
EBS snapshots preserve block data and do not interpret audio.
WAF evaluates web requests and does not process speech.

feedback.reason: Amazon Transcribe converts speech to text through a managed service and supports application-controlled transcript processing.

options.text: Use Amazon Transcribe for managed speech-to-text processing, with secure storage, language and vocabulary configuration, and transcript quality controls.
Use Amazon Polly because text-to-speech synthesis automatically creates accurate transcripts from audio recordings.
Use Amazon EBS snapshots because block-storage backups expose spoken words as searchable text.
Use AWS WAF because web request inspection converts call audio into transcripts.

prompt: A contact center stores call recordings and needs searchable transcripts without operating speech-recognition servers. Which service should the architect evaluate?

constraints: The source is text.
The output is synthesized speech.
The application must manage caching, authorization, and any voice or language requirements.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Voice availability, pronunciation, latency, cost, caching, and content access policy remain application design concerns.
details.errorCorrection: Transcribe converts speech to text, VPC provides networking, and Inspector identifies security issues.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Polly accepts text and returns synthesized audio using a selected voice and supported language or speech configuration.
details.scenarioApplication: The application invokes Polly for uncached content, stores authorized audio where appropriate, and avoids regenerating identical content unnecessarily.

messages.text: Transcribe processes speech into text rather than text into speech.
VPC networking does not synthesize audio.
Inspector findings are security data and not a text-to-speech engine.

feedback.reason: Amazon Polly is purpose-built for managed text-to-speech synthesis.

options.text: Use Amazon Polly to synthesize speech from text, then control access and cache generated audio according to content and latency requirements.
Use Amazon Transcribe because speech-to-text is the required direction for converting an article into audio.
Use Amazon VPC because subnets automatically render text into spoken audio.
Use Amazon Inspector because vulnerability findings can be played as article audio without a synthesis service.

prompt: A reading application must turn article text into spoken audio on demand and return the audio to a client. Which service is the direct fit?

constraints: The source and target languages are supported by the service.
The original and translated messages must be retained separately.
Translation quality must be checked for the business domain.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Supported languages, terminology, quality, privacy, latency, and human review requirements must be validated for the domain.
details.errorCorrection: Polly synthesizes audio, replication copies bytes, and load balancers route traffic without translating payloads.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Translate accepts text with source and target language configuration and returns a translated result that the application can store and review.
details.scenarioApplication: The portal records the immutable source, translated output, language metadata, and any review status so the original remains available for audit.

messages.text: Polly is text-to-speech and does not provide text translation as its primary contract.
Replication preserves object content and does not translate it.
A load balancer routes requests and does not transform natural-language content.

feedback.reason: Amazon Translate provides managed text translation and fits the stated language-conversion workload.

options.text: Use Amazon Translate for managed text translation, while retaining the source text and applying domain-specific quality and privacy controls.
Use Amazon Polly because speech synthesis translates text between languages without a translation operation.
Use Amazon S3 replication because copying an object to another Region changes the language of its contents.
Use an Application Load Balancer listener rule because routing a request to another target translates its body.

prompt: A customer portal must translate support messages between supported languages while preserving the original message for audit. Which service should be evaluated?

constraints: The input is natural-language text.
The output informs routing rather than replacing a final human decision.
Customer text is sensitive and must be governed.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Language coverage, domain accuracy, confidence interpretation, privacy, and human review should be explicit.
details.errorCorrection: Rekognition analyzes visual content, EBS stores blocks, and Route 53 routes DNS requests.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Comprehend analyzes supported text and returns language insights that an application can use as signals in a larger workflow.
details.scenarioApplication: The router uses the result to prioritize or select a queue, but keeps a path for uncertainty and does not expose raw sensitive text unnecessarily.

messages.text: Rekognition is for image and video analysis, not general text sentiment classification.
EBS stores data but does not analyze language.
DNS policies have no text-understanding capability.

feedback.reason: Amazon Comprehend is designed for managed natural-language analysis such as sentiment and entity detection.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon Comprehend for managed natural-language analysis, then define confidence thresholds, privacy controls, and review behavior.
Use Amazon Rekognition because image labeling APIs automatically understand the sentiment of text messages.
Use Amazon EBS because block storage can classify entities without an inference operation.
Use Amazon Route 53 because DNS routing policies assign sentiment labels to customer messages.

prompt: A support team wants to identify sentiment and entities in customer messages before routing them to specialized queues. Which service is the most direct fit?

constraints: The source is file-based media.
Transcoding can be asynchronous and must be tracked as a job.
Outputs should be stored and delivered independently of the worker.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Output profiles, processing cost, job duration, input validation, retries, and content protection remain part of the workflow design.
details.errorCorrection: DynamoDB stores data, CloudTrail records events, and S3 lifecycle policies manage storage transitions rather than codecs.
details.mechanismOrProperty: MediaConvert creates transcoding jobs from source media and produces configured outputs that can be stored in AWS storage and delivered by another service.
details.scenarioApplication: The platform submits a job after upload, records job state, handles failures or retries, and publishes only completed renditions.

messages.text: A database stores records and does not transcode media.
CloudTrail provides audit history and does not create video renditions.
Lifecycle rules change storage management and do not transform video codecs.

feedback.reason: MediaConvert is a managed service for file-based media transcoding and supports job-oriented processing.

options.text: Use AWS Elemental MediaConvert for managed file-based transcoding jobs, with S3 input and output, job status handling, and delivery controls.
Use Amazon DynamoDB as the transcoder because a table can change codecs when an item is written.
Use Amazon CloudTrail because audit events automatically produce all required video renditions.
Use an S3 lifecycle rule because changing storage class performs codec conversion.

prompt: A video platform receives source files in varied formats and must create several playback renditions asynchronously. Which service should the architect evaluate?

constraints: The workload is live streaming rather than file transcoding.
Latency and viewer scale matter.
The application must control channel and viewer experience behavior.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Live streaming still requires ingest, latency, viewer access, moderation, recording, content rights, and regional availability decisions.
details.errorCorrection: EFS is shared file storage, RDS replicas serve database reads, and Config evaluates configuration compliance.
details.mechanismOrProperty: IVS provides live streaming primitives and playback endpoints while the application manages channel access, user experience, moderation, and related content workflows.
details.scenarioApplication: The platform creates or selects channels, protects stream keys and playback access, and handles recording or chat according to product requirements.

messages.text: EFS provides file storage and is not a live video delivery platform.
RDS replicas return database results and do not distribute encoded media streams.
AWS Config records resource configuration and compliance, not live media.

feedback.reason: Amazon IVS is purpose-built for managed live video streaming and channel-oriented playback.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon IVS for managed live streaming channels and playback, then design authentication, moderation, recording, and scaling behavior around the stream.
Use Amazon EFS as the live-video distribution service because shared files automatically provide low-latency streaming to viewers.
Use Amazon RDS read replicas as video channels because database replicas deliver encoded media to browsers.
Use AWS Config because resource compliance evaluations are equivalent to live media delivery.

prompt: A creator platform needs managed low-latency live video delivery with chat and channel lifecycle APIs. Which service is the most direct candidate?

constraints: Relationship traversal is the dominant access pattern.
The team wants a managed graph database.
The design must still address graph scale, query patterns, and recovery.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A graph model is valuable when traversal dominates; it is not a universal replacement for transactional, document, or analytical stores.
details.errorCorrection: S3 prefixes navigate objects, a cache is not an authoritative durable graph, and CloudFront does not compute graph paths.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A graph database models entities and edges directly, allowing relationship-oriented queries that would otherwise require complex joins or application-side traversal.
details.scenarioApplication: The investigator queries connected accounts and devices through graph relationships while the team defines indexes, query limits, backups, and data ingestion behavior.

messages.text: Object prefixes do not provide graph edges or arbitrary relationship traversal.
A cache can accelerate reads but cannot be the sole durable graph source.
CloudFront distributes content and does not execute graph queries.

feedback.reason: Neptune is designed for graph workloads in which relationships and traversals are first-class access patterns.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon Neptune for a managed graph data model that represents vertices and relationships and supports graph queries.
Choose S3 objects as the graph engine because object prefixes automatically traverse arbitrary relationships and hops.
Choose ElastiCache as the only authoritative graph store because cache keys guarantee durable relationship traversal.
Choose CloudFront because edge locations automatically calculate graph paths between fraud entities.

prompt: A fraud investigation application must traverse relationships among accounts, devices, merchants, and transactions across many hops. Which data model should be evaluated first?

constraints: The data is append-oriented time-series telemetry.
Queries are primarily time-window and aggregation queries.
Retention and cost behavior must be explicit.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: The architect must validate cardinality, query shape, retention cost, late data, ingestion reliability, and aggregation requirements.
details.errorCorrection: Cognito manages identities, WAF filters requests, and ECR stores container images.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A time-series service organizes records around timestamps and supports time-oriented ingestion, queries, and retention tiers.
details.scenarioApplication: The fleet writes measurements with device and time dimensions, and operators query recent windows while older data follows the selected retention policy.

messages.text: Cognito provides identity management and is not a telemetry database.
WAF metrics are operational observations and not a general time-series data model for device readings.
ECR stores container images and has no sensor time-series query model.

feedback.reason: Timestream is purpose-built for time-series data and supports the stated telemetry access pattern.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon Timestream for managed time-series ingestion, time-based queries, and configurable retention behavior.
Use Amazon Cognito as the telemetry database because user pools automatically aggregate measurements by timestamp.
Use Amazon WAF because web ACL metrics become a general-purpose time-series store for every device.
Use Amazon ECR because container image tags are the correct durable model for sensor readings.

prompt: An IoT fleet emits timestamped temperature and battery measurements continuously, and operators need time-window queries and retention tiers. Which service should be evaluated?

constraints: The workload uses a document data model and compatible client behavior.
The migration must be tested against actual features and versions.
The team wants managed database operations.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Compatibility does not mean identical behavior; unsupported features, performance, version, availability, and migration constraints must be tested.
details.errorCorrection: Neptune is for graph relationships, SQS is a message transport, and CloudWatch Logs is an observability store.
details.mechanismOrProperty: DocumentDB provides a managed document database interface with a documented compatibility scope and operational characteristics.
details.scenarioApplication: The migration team inventories commands, indexes, drivers, transactions, aggregation behavior, and performance before selecting the service and cutover plan.

messages.text: A document workload is not automatically a graph workload; graph selection depends on relationship traversal needs.
SQS transports messages and does not provide a document query or indexing model.
Logs are designed for observations and retention, not transactional document persistence.

feedback.reason: DocumentDB is a candidate for document workloads that need MongoDB compatibility, but compatibility must be validated rather than assumed.

options.text: Evaluate Amazon DocumentDB compatibility and feature coverage, then test the application and design backup, scaling, and availability behavior.
Choose Amazon Neptune automatically because every JSON document is a graph and requires graph traversal.
Choose Amazon SQS as the document database because messages preserve document queries and indexes indefinitely.
Choose Amazon CloudWatch Logs as the system of record because log events provide a complete document database API.

prompt: A team is migrating a document application that uses MongoDB-compatible APIs and wants a managed AWS database with minimal application-model change. Which service is a candidate?

constraints: Local processing and intermittent connectivity are required.
Device credentials and updates must be managed securely.
Only selected data should be synchronized to the cloud.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Edge deployments require device lifecycle, update, observability, physical security, storage, and conflict or replay behavior to be designed.
details.errorCorrection: A public database round trip violates the offline requirement, CloudFront distributes content rather than running arbitrary device workloads, and IAM policies are not runtimes.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Greengrass deploys components to edge devices and can integrate local processing with AWS IoT connectivity and cloud synchronization.
details.scenarioApplication: The factory evaluates rules locally, stores or buffers selected results, authenticates devices, and synchronizes data when connectivity returns.

messages.text: A required cloud round trip fails when connectivity is intermittent and expands the device attack surface.
CloudFront is a content-delivery service and cannot replace an edge application runtime.
IAM authorizes actions but does not execute sensor processing or provide a device runtime.

feedback.reason: Greengrass provides an AWS-managed edge runtime for local components and processing when cloud connectivity is intermittent.

options.text: Evaluate AWS IoT Greengrass for edge components and local processing, with IoT connectivity, secure deployment, buffering, and explicit synchronization behavior.
Place every device operation behind a public database and require a round trip to the Region for every sensor decision.
Use CloudFront as the device runtime because cached web objects continue to execute arbitrary factory control code offline.
Use an IAM policy alone as the edge application because authorization rules process sensor data without a runtime.

prompt: Factory devices must process sensor data locally during intermittent connectivity and synchronize selected results with AWS when the connection returns. Which architecture should be evaluated?

constraints: The custom model must demonstrate measurable quality improvement.
The team wants managed training and deployment primitives.
The model lifecycle, data security, and rollback process must be owned explicitly.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Customization can improve domain performance but adds data, training, serving, monitoring, security, and lifecycle responsibilities.
details.errorCorrection: Immediate custom adoption without evidence increases risk, schemas do not replace model evaluation, and cached predictions are not inference.
details.mechanismOrProperty: A baseline establishes whether custom training improves the required metric; SageMaker can provide managed training and hosting primitives without requiring a team-built platform.
details.scenarioApplication: The team runs representative benchmarks, defines promotion and rollback gates, and only accepts the operational cost of a custom model when the improvement is material.

messages.text: Without a baseline and lifecycle controls, the team cannot show the custom model is worth its operational cost.
A schema stores structured data and does not provide predictive behavior or evaluation.
A cache can serve a prior result but cannot adapt to a new input as a model does.

feedback.reason: The decision should compare managed-service quality with the value of customization, then use managed ML infrastructure where a custom model is justified.

options.text: Benchmark a managed API first, and if the domain gap justifies customization, use SageMaker AI managed training and hosting rather than operating the platform from scratch.
Adopt a custom model immediately without a baseline, evaluation metric, rollback plan, or ownership for serving operations.
Assume a database schema can encode domain behavior and eliminate the need for model evaluation.
Use a CDN cache as the model because returning the last prediction is always equivalent to inference.

prompt: A company has a highly domain-specific prediction target and enough labeled data to improve accuracy beyond a managed API, but it lacks a serving platform. What is the most balanced direction?

constraints: The model is already deployed.
Input and outcome data can be observed over time.
The system must detect degradation before it silently affects customers.

details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Monitoring and retraining add cost and data-governance work, but silent model degradation is an explicit availability and correctness risk.
details.errorCorrection: Removing observability hides degradation, an unlimited timeout harms availability, and deleting evidence prevents evaluation and retraining.
details.mechanismOrProperty: Operational controls connect inference metrics and feedback to quality checks, retraining decisions, and controlled model deployment.
details.scenarioApplication: The team measures latency, errors, input distribution, and eventual outcomes, then retrains and promotes a candidate only when defined gates pass.

messages.text: Without metrics the team cannot detect operational or quality degradation.
Longer timeouts do not improve model quality and can exhaust callers and endpoint capacity.
Historical data and outcomes are needed to investigate, evaluate, and improve model behavior.

feedback.reason: Production ML needs an observable lifecycle because data and model behavior can change after deployment.

options.text: Instrument the inference path and establish monitoring, feedback data, drift or quality checks, retraining criteria, and a safe model promotion or rollback process.
Disable all metrics because monitoring changes the model and therefore cannot be used in production.
Increase the endpoint timeout indefinitely so degraded predictions have more time to become accurate.
Delete the training data after deployment because a deployed model never needs evidence for evaluation.

prompt: An ML-backed API has acceptable offline accuracy but its production predictions are becoming less useful as customer behavior changes. Which architectural control is most important?
